name: Jade Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on Ridgeway Farm, my husband's family place, about a hundred and twenty hectares with sheep, a few beef cattle, laying hens, potatoes and a farm shop by the road. His brother Hiro runs the farm, and I run the shop and help wherever I'm told, feeding the hens, grading potatoes, moving sheep with a bucket. I'm in at seven for the hens, open the shop at nine, and close at five, then it's the till, the orders and the posts online.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you help where you're told. How new is this for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years. For thirty years I was a clerk at the bank branch in Marlow, and when they closed it I was offered a job in a call centre an hour away. Kenji, my husband, said come home, the family needs you, and his brother needed someone for the shop. So I'm the newest pair of hands, and the farm pays me what it can, which isn't much.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Better than when I came, I'm proud of that. I use an AI assistant every single day, for the shop's posts, the price labels, working out what sells on a Saturday, even writing the little cards about where the eggs come from. Sales are up about a fifth. But I'm still hopeless with the sheep, and we've less than a month of money put by, because every spare penny goes back into the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best thing since the cash register, and I'd say it to anyone. At the Women's Institute meeting last month I showed six ladies how to make a menu card with it. Two of them now use it for their church newsletters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is a good picture for us. A small shop like ours gets the same clever help as the big supermarkets, for almost nothing. If nothing else changes, I can keep growing the shop slowly and maybe pay myself a bit more next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the shop harder. I'd start a weekly box of veg and eggs for local families, ordered through a simple page the AI helps me build, delivered on Fridays. I'd aim for forty boxes by the summer. And I'd ask Hiro for a small raise once the boxes are paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit eager, like the first warm day in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has using AI ever caused a problem in the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once. It wrote a lovely card for our honey saying it was from wildflower meadows, and our bees mostly sit next to a field of oilseed rape. A customer who keeps bees laughed at me. Now I read every word before it goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Hiro feel about you using it so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He calls it my little friend, and not kindly at first. Then I showed him that it worked out which days we waste the most bread, and he went quiet. He still won't use it himself. He says a farmer should keep his numbers in his head.

S0.say: I'd say it's the best thing since the cash register. I showed six ladies at the Women's Institute how to make a menu card with it.
S0.think: This is a good picture for us, because a small shop gets the same clever help as the supermarkets for almost nothing. I could grow the shop slowly and pay myself a bit more.
S0.do: Starts a weekly veg and egg box for local families through a simple web page, aiming for forty boxes by summer. Asks her brother-in-law for a small raise once the boxes pay.
S0.feel: Calm and eager, like the first warm day in spring.
S0.quote: It wrote a lovely card for our honey saying it was from wildflower meadows, and our bees mostly sit next to a field of oilseed rape.
S0.fieldNote: Jade is an energetic late starter who sees AI as a way for a small family business to compete. The honey story showed her catching the tool's mistakes, and her brother-in-law's quiet change of heart was telling. She ties growth directly to a modest raise for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible. Businesses should be free to adopt things at their own pace. But I'd say families and small firms like ours should keep taking on young people, because that's how you pass things on. Our nephew Ren is seventeen and he'll learn this farm whether there's AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think slow suits a farm like ours, and suits me. I'd keep improving the shop year by year. My worry is the other end, the bank. I know from Marlow that slow change empties branches one desk at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take Ren on in the shop on Saturdays, paid, and teach him the AI side while Hiro teaches him the sheep. I'd join the local farm shop network and share what works. And I'd start a little savings pot for myself, ten a week, because I've never had one of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of old sadness about the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'one desk at a time'. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I started at Marlow there were nine of us. Every couple of years someone retired and the desk just went. By the end it was three of us and a machine in the wall. Nobody was sacked, it just got quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a savings pot of your own, rather than the family's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because at fifty-eight, I've given everything to one family business or another. I love them. But my mother always said a woman should have a little purse of her own, and I never listened. I'd listen now.

S1.say: I'd say businesses should be free to adopt things at their own pace, but families and small firms should keep taking on young people to pass things on.
S1.think: Slow suits a farm like ours and suits me. My worry is the other end, because I know from the bank that slow change empties branches one desk at a time.
S1.do: Takes her teenage nephew on in the shop on paid Saturdays to learn the AI side alongside the sheep. Joins the local farm shop network and starts a ten-a-week savings pot of her own.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with some old sadness about the bank.
S1.quote: By the end it was three of us and a machine in the wall. Nobody was sacked, it just got quieter.
S1.fieldNote: She believes in families passing skills on, and wants her nephew to learn both the sheep and the AI. Her bank memories gave a quiet, clear picture of slow change. The private savings pot, after her mother's advice, was a small but telling detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will have to adapt, the way I did when the bank closed. And I'd say the answer is work and training, not just payments, because a job gives you more than money. I'd say it to anyone, though I'd say it gently to people who'd just lost their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two things. Office people losing jobs means fewer people with money to spend on our nice eggs and lamb, which would hurt the shop. And my son Kai works in an office doing customer support for a phone company, which is just the kind of job you mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep prices steady on the basics, eggs, potatoes, bread, and push the cheaper boxes, so people still come in when money's tight. I'd ring Kai and tell him to learn to run those AI assistants himself, before someone else does. And I'd offer him Saturdays in the shop if things went wrong, at whatever we could pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. For Kai, and for the till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Kai say if you told him to learn the assistants?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, Mum, you're the one who uses it for everything, you learn it. I'd say I already have, which is why I'm telling you. He'd sigh, but he'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said work, not payments. If Kai lost his job, would you want him to claim benefits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a short while, yes, to bridge him. But I'd want him working as soon as possible, even in the shop. Sitting at home does something to a young man, I've seen it with my nephew's friends.

S2.say: I'd say people will have to adapt, as I did when the bank closed, and the answer is work and training more than payments. I'd say it gently to those just laid off.
S2.think: Office layoffs would mean fewer people spending on our eggs and lamb, which hurts the shop. And my son does customer support in an office, exactly that kind of job.
S2.do: Holds prices on basics and pushes cheaper boxes to keep customers coming. Tells her son to learn to run AI assistants and offers him paid Saturdays in the shop if he loses his job.
S2.feel: Uneasy, for her son and for the till.
S2.quote: Uneasy. For Kai, and for the till.
S2.fieldNote: Her traditional view of work over payments softened into 'a short bridge, then work'. She saw the shop's risk clearly through her customers' spending. Her son's job brought the picture home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built things deserve their rewards, but they should invest them here, in real businesses and real places, not just in shares and second houses. And I'd say the crisis needs calm people, not shouting. Family, church, local business, that's the steady ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one could be good for the shop and bad for the town. Rich people with booming shares buy weekend cottages round here, and they love a farm shop, they'd pay double for our lamb. But the young families get priced out, and they're the ones who've kept us going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add a higher-end line, lamb boxes, hampers, the things weekend people buy, while keeping the cheap basics for locals. I'd use the AI to price both and keep them separate. And I'd talk to Hiro about the farm cottage we rent out, and whether we let it to a local family at a fair rent instead of to holiday people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a businesswoman's itch. I know that's an awkward mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Letting the cottage to a local family would cost you money. Would Hiro agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not happily. He'd do the sums and see holiday lets make three times as much. But his son Ren wants to farm here, and he'll need neighbours who aren't only here at weekends. I'd make that case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said awkward mix. What's awkward about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd be making money from the same thing that's hurting people I go to church with. I'd tell myself I'm keeping the farm alive. That's true. It's also convenient.

S3.say: I'd say the people who built things deserve their rewards but should invest them in real local businesses, not just shares and second houses. The crisis needs calm people.
S3.think: This could be good for the shop and bad for the town. Weekend-home buyers would pay double for our lamb, but young local families would be priced out.
S3.do: Adds a higher-priced line of lamb boxes and hampers for weekend visitors while keeping cheap basics for locals, using AI to price both. Pushes to let the farm cottage to a local family at a fair rent.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a businesswoman's itch she admits is an awkward mix.
S3.quote: I'd tell myself I'm keeping the farm alive. That's true. It's also convenient.
S3.fieldNote: She was strikingly honest about profiting from a boom that hurts her neighbours. Her plan balanced the two with separate products for weekend buyers and locals. She'd argue for the local family in the cottage for the sake of the farm's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on a family farm could be a blessing if the family owns them and decides. I'd say small farms need fair access, so it's not just the big estates who get them. And I'd say the shop counter is one place people will still want a human face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my farm jobs would go, the hens, the grading, maybe the sheep work, and I'm the least skilled at those anyway. But the shop is my bit, and I think people would want a person there even more. The risk is money: robots cost a fortune, and if Hiro borrows to buy them, the whole family's tied to the debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Hiro and Kenji and plan it properly, maybe one robot shared with two neighbouring farms rather than buying our own. I'd let the farm jobs go and put all my time into the shop and the boxes, perhaps add a café corner. I'd use the AI to compare every robot's price and running costs before anyone signs anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my job so much, for the family's money and for my old bank friends. But a bit hopeful too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the friend from the bank you'd think of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pauline, who sat next to me for twenty years. She went to a supermarket warehouse after the branch closed. In your picture, the warehouse goes too. I'd ring her and offer her a job in the café, even if it's only two days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd share one robot between three farms. Would the neighbours trust that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd grumble. Farmers don't share easily, everyone wants their own tractor. But nobody round here can afford one alone, so it's share or don't have one. We share a bull already, I tell them, a robot's less trouble than the bull.

S4.say: I'd say robots could be a blessing on a family farm if the family owns and decides, and small farms need fair access, not just big estates. The shop counter will still want a human face.
S4.think: My farm jobs would go, and I'm least skilled at those anyway, but people would want a person in the shop even more. The real risk is the family getting tied to a big robot debt.
S4.do: Plans with the family to share one robot with two neighbouring farms instead of buying alone, using AI to compare costs. Drops the farm jobs to focus on the shop and boxes, possibly adding a café corner.
S4.feel: Anxious for the family's money and her old bank colleagues, but a bit hopeful too.
S4.quote: We share a bull already, I tell them, a robot's less trouble than the bull.
S4.fieldNote: Even in the robot picture she was looking for the opening, betting the shop counter stays human. Her worry was debt across the family, and her answer, sharing a robot like they share a bull, was very practical. She'd use the café to help an old bank friend.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, for the money. If Hiro borrows for robots and the prices drop, the whole family goes down together, and I'm not sure I could save it with eggs and hampers. What would help is fair loans for small farms to share machines, and help for local shops to compete. Not handouts, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the counter. Half the people who come in don't need eggs, they need a chat. A widower comes in every day for one loaf. A robot won't notice when he doesn't come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's a good point. Anything else?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that at fifty-eight I'm the new girl on the farm, and I'm the one who uses the computer most. Life's funny like that.

headlineQuote: We share a bull already, I tell them, a robot's less trouble than the bull.
portrait: Jade Ito is 58 and for two years has run the farm shop and helped out on her husband's family's mixed farm, after thirty years as a bank clerk ended when her branch closed. She's paid little, has less than a month saved and uses an AI assistant every day for the shop, which has lifted sales by about a fifth, while admitting she's hopeless with the sheep. Her traditional values show in her trust in family, church and work over payments, but she's honest about the awkward fact that a boom in weekend homes would help her shop while hurting her neighbours. In the robot picture she happily gives up the farm jobs, bets on the human shop counter, and worries most about the family taking on robot debt.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because if the family borrows for robots and prices fall, they all go down together.
whatWouldHelp: Fair loans for small farms to share machines and help for local shops to compete, which she calls a fair start, not a handout.
